paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a geometric data structure can serve as a useful neural network classifier. Its starting point is the bumptree, a structure designed to make a collection of functions over Euclidean space efficiently accessible. Here, Euclidean space is the coordinate space in which the inputs are represented.

The authors modify that structure and use it to assign inputs to classes. This connects two concerns that are often considered separately: how functions are organized for efficient access, and how a learning system uses them to make classification decisions. The modification turns the bumptree into a candidate network architecture.

The study compares the resulting classifier with radial basis function networks and a standard multilayer perceptron across several classification tasks. Its contribution is therefore both architectural and comparative: it introduces a modified structure and evaluates it alongside established network types. The supplied abstract identifies the comparison but does not state which method performs best, so it supports no overall ranking.
neurips-1993-a-comparative-study-of-a-mo.tldr: The paper adapts a bumptree geometric structure into a classifier and compares it with radial basis function networks and multilayer perceptrons.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a representation problem in predicting biological activity: the features describing a compound can change with its position or orientation. A learning system must therefore deal with variation caused by how an example is posed, alongside variation relevant to the activity being predicted.

Dynamic reposing tackles this by alternating between learning and repositioning. It first trains a neural network, then changes the poses of the examples to increase the network's predicted outputs. New networks and new poses are repeatedly computed until both settle. The input representation and the prediction model are consequently adjusted together.

The authors compare this procedure with tangent distance, a method used to address pose variation in handwritten character recognition. Their application is activity prediction for musk compounds. The abstract begins describing a 20-fold cross-validation but ends before reporting its outcome. The supported contribution is the comparison of two ways to handle pose dependence; the supplied evidence does not establish a winning method.
neurips-1993-a-comparison-of-dynamic-rep.tldr: The paper compares iterative pose adjustment with tangent distance for predicting the biological activity of musk compounds.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to fit a Hodgkin–Huxley type neuron model to a recorded voltage trajectory. Rather than choosing the model's physiological parameters entirely by hand, the authors derive a gradient descent procedure related to learning algorithms for recurrent neural networks operating in continuous time.

The target is the membrane potential as it changes over time. The adjustable quantities include maximal conductances, activation thresholds and slopes, and time constants. These parameters describe how the modeled electrical currents respond and evolve. The abstract reports successful estimation, showing that observed voltage dynamics can guide the fitting of this detailed neuron model.

The method is applied to slow oscillations without spikes in an identified lobster stomatogastric neuron. A model containing three ionic currents is trained on experimental recordings. The resulting model reveals a previously unrecognized role for the A-current in oscillations below −50 mV. The significance is that fitting the dynamics also yields a specific proposed contribution of an ionic current.
neurips-1993-a-hodgkin-huxley-type-neuro.tldr: A gradient descent method fits a detailed neuron model to voltage recordings and reveals a role for the A-current in slow oscillations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between recurrent neural networks and finite-state machines. A recurrent network normally moves through a continuous range of internal states, while a finite-state machine operates using a finite collection of distinct states. Learning the right outputs does not automatically make those internal representations discrete.

The proposed architecture, DOLCE, combines a recurrent network trained by gradient descent with adaptive clustering of its state space. Its explicit assumption is that the task requires finitely many discrete states and that the network's observed state is a noisy version of one of them. The noise is attributed to inaccurate weights.

Clustering allows discrete states to develop as training proceeds. DOLCE recovers the state with the highest posterior probability from the noisy network state, tying the continuous learning process to the assumed discrete structure. Simulations report substantially improved generalization over earlier neural approaches to finite-state-machine induction. The result supports making the task's state structure part of the architecture when that finite-state assumption applies.
neurips-1993-a-unified-gradient-descent-.tldr: DOLCE combines recurrent-network learning with adaptive state clustering to improve generalization when learning finite-state machines.

paragraphs: The paper describes a system that locates the destination address on a piece of mail. Finding text alone is insufficient because an image may also contain advertising, drawings, and dirt. The system analyzes the page layout to separate these elements and identify which text belongs to the address.

It also determines whether the writing is handwritten or machine printed, measures the tilt of the text lines, and cleans noisy images. These functions address several aspects of preparing a mail image for subsequent processing. The implementation uses modular hardware combining two neural network chips, a processor board, and two digital signal processors.

Tests involve more than 100,000 images, and the reported processing speed exceeds four images per second. Correct address location ranges from 85% for very noisy images to more than 98% for cleaner ones. Image quality is thus a stated influence on performance. The results demonstrate a working, high-throughput location system whose reliability varies with the condition of its input.
neurips-1993-address-block-location-with.tldr: A neural hardware system locates mail addresses at over four images per second, with accuracy ranging from 85% to over 98% depending on image quality.

paragraphs: The paper offers a functional interpretation of the complicated spikes and voltage plateaus recorded inside dendrites. The authors argue that these events can reflect an underlying mechanism for proportionally amplifying electrical input. Its proposed purpose is to compensate for signal losses as current travels through the neuron's branching structure.

They examine synaptic inputs arriving in superficial cortical layers at the distant dendrites of a layer 5 pyramidal neuron. Using a reconstruction grounded in anatomy and electrical measurements, they derive and simulate conductance properties that strengthen these inputs while making the relationship between input and amplified current more linear.

The proposed amplification is graded, meaning that its strength varies with the input rather than being described only as an all-or-nothing event. It depends on potassium conductance in the apical tuft and calcium conductances in the apical trunk. The study therefore links specific conductances in different dendritic locations to a common computational role: preserving the influence of distant synaptic inputs through proportional amplification.
neurips-1993-amplifying-and-linearizing-.tldr: The paper models how potassium and calcium conductances could proportionally amplify distant synaptic inputs and offset electrical losses in pyramidal-cell dendrites.

paragraphs: The paper examines short-term memory as a component of neural networks that process information changing over time. In this setting, the current input is only part of the information available to the system. A memory provides a way for earlier inputs to remain relevant during ongoing processing.

The authors present a model for linear memories and discuss ways of incorporating memory into connectionist architectures. These are complementary design questions: what mathematical form the memory takes, and how it becomes part of the network. Treating memory explicitly makes its role in temporal processing available for analysis rather than leaving it implicit in the overall architecture.

The paper also compares different memory types and identifies the distinguishing characteristic of each. Its emphasis is therefore on understanding memory choices and their integration, rather than reporting a single application result. The contribution is a framework for examining how a network retains recent information and how alternative memory models differ as components of a time-dependent processing system.
neurips-1993-analysis-of-short-term-memo.tldr: The paper models linear short-term memories and compares ways of incorporating memory into neural networks for time-varying information.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to interpret networks built by cascade-correlation learning. These networks contain connections that cut across a conventional hidden-layer organization. Looking only at hidden-unit activations can therefore miss how units actually influence the output, making ordinary activation-based analysis insufficient.

The method extends contribution analysis. For each input pattern, a unit's contribution combines its activation, its connection weight to the output, and the sign of the desired output. This relates a unit's activity to the direction and strength of its output influence. Contributions are collected across patterns, and principal components analysis extracts their main shared variations.

The authors apply the analysis to continuous XOR, arithmetic comparison, and separating two interlocking spirals. In all three problems, it produces useful interpretations that remain consistent across several networks. The result suggests that examining coordinated output contributions can reveal common features of learned solutions even when the architecture lacks a simple layer-by-layer structure and individual activations are difficult to interpret.
neurips-1993-analyzing-cross-connected-n.tldr: Contribution analysis and principal components analysis reveal consistent patterns in how cross-connected networks solve three classification problems.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a high-dimensional function when the learner can influence where new data come from. This makes data collection part of the learning problem. The challenge is to explore toward a goal while maintaining the prediction accuracy needed during that exploration.

The method represents the function using locally weighted regression, building predictions from local models. Architectural choices, including distance measures, also vary with the query point rather than remaining fixed everywhere. Statistical tests determine when a local model is sufficiently accurate and the learner should begin sampling another area.

Exploration proceeds by gradually moving a center of exploration along the boundary of the region already supported by data. Local prediction accuracy controls how quickly that center moves. This connects confidence in current predictions directly to the pace of collecting new experience. Simulations and a real robot learning a complex juggling task illustrate the approach, showing how local model assessment can guide goal-directed exploration under ongoing accuracy requirements.
neurips-1993-assessing-the-quality-of-le.tldr: Local prediction-quality tests guide where and how quickly a learner explores, with demonstrations including a robot learning to juggle.

paragraphs: The paper presents a system for learning, tracking, and recognizing hand gestures from a conventional camera. It does not require instrumented gloves or additional sensors. The central task is to turn the recorded appearance and motion of a hand into a compact representation suitable for gesture classification.

An unsupervised clustering procedure discovers views that describe aspects of the hand relevant to the trained gestures. Similarity is measured using normalized correlation networks together with dynamic time warping for temporal comparisons. Spatial and temporal views are computed separately, and the combined pattern of responses across these units forms a low-dimensional description of the input.

A supervised stage then learns from labeled outputs of those spatial and temporal units. Representation discovery and gesture labeling thus play distinct roles in the system: one organizes the visual observations, while the other maps their responses to gesture categories. The authors report correct real-time classification using a low-cost image processing accelerator, demonstrating the practical use of this combined representation.
neurips-1993-classifying-hand-gestures-w.tldr: A camera-based gesture system learns compact spatial and temporal representations and uses them for real-time supervised classification.

paragraphs: The paper proposes improving a next-step time-series predictor by learning from its mistakes. After training an initial network, the authors examine the differences between its predictions and the training observations. These residuals form a second time series that can itself be modeled.

A secondary network learns that residual series, and its output supplies a correction to the first network's prediction. The combined pair becomes the new predictor. This separates the learning task into an initial prediction problem and a correction problem, allowing the second network to focus directly on structure left in the first network's errors.

The authors demonstrate the approach on sunspot data and report that the two-stage procedure succeeds. They also interpret its small corrections through a Taylor expansion of a more complex network containing the combined system. That more complex network is harder to train and performs worse in their comparison. The finding highlights that training the prediction and correction stages separately can matter even when a larger model encompasses their combined behavior.
neurips-1993-combined-neural-networks-fo.tldr: Training a second network on a predictor's residual errors improves sunspot forecasting and outperforms a related, harder-to-train complex network.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning methods that learn an environment model and use it to compute control policies. These are indirect adaptive methods: experience updates the model, and planning uses the latest model. This approach is relevant when the controlled environment is represented as a Markov process but its dynamics are initially unknown.

The authors establish a convergence result for indirect adaptive asynchronous value iteration. The stated setting stores the value function in a lookup table. The result therefore concerns this explicit representation of values, rather than an unspecified function approximator. It gives a theoretical basis for a family of algorithms that combine model learning with value updates.

The theorem implies convergence for existing methods including adaptive real-time dynamic programming and prioritized sweeping. Its significance is to strengthen the foundations of model-based learning while the environment model is still being adapted. The authors also question whether direct methods deserve practical preference, but the abstract does not claim that the convergence result establishes a performance advantage over them.
neurips-1993-convergence-of-indirect-ada.tldr: The paper proves convergence for a family of model-based asynchronous value-iteration algorithms using tabular value functions.

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning from sequences when an output depends on information received much earlier. Such tasks require long-term context, but training recurrent networks to use that context presents both practical and theoretical difficulties. The central issue is assigning learning credit across the interval separating relevant inputs and outputs.

The authors begin with a mathematical analysis and then consider alternative learning algorithms and architectures. They compare these alternatives on tasks where the length of the input-output dependency can be controlled. Making that interval adjustable lets the study examine the specific challenge of learning across time, rather than treating sequence learning as a single undifferentiated capability.

The new algorithms show qualitatively better performance than backpropagation in the reported comparisons. This finding supports investigating changes to both learning procedures and network structure when distant context is necessary. The contribution combines an analysis of the training difficulty with controlled comparisons of alternatives, linking the theoretical problem of temporal credit assignment to observed differences in sequence-learning behavior.
neurips-1993-credit-assignment-through-t.tldr: The paper analyzes long-term temporal credit assignment and reports alternatives that perform qualitatively better than backpropagation on controlled sequence tasks.

paragraphs: The paper approaches online cursive handwriting recognition by first changing how the pen trajectory is represented. A dynamic encoding converts the recorded movement into a compact sequence of discrete motor-control symbols. This representation removes much of the script's redundancy while retaining most of the information needed to interpret it.

The second phase trains adaptive probabilistic acyclic automata on those symbol sequences. These models represent important components of writing trajectories, such as letters. The authors introduce an efficient learning algorithm for the automata and use the learned models to locate letter-like components and divide cursive writing into meaningful segments.

The experiments report that more than 90% of letters are correctly located and identified before applying a higher-level language model. That result attributes substantial recognition capability to the trajectory representation and learned component models themselves. The authors also report efficient training and recognition compared with other modeling methods, together with online adaptation to different writers and styles. The approach thus joins compact movement encoding with adaptable probabilistic recognition.
neurips-1993-decoding-cursive-scripts-02.tldr: Compact motor-control encoding and probabilistic automata identify over 90% of cursive letters before higher-level language modeling.

paragraphs: The paper models how animals can learn useful foraging strategies when outcomes are uncertain. Predicting future consequences can help an animal choose its next action and prepare for reward or punishment. The authors seek a neural mechanism connecting those predictions with both behavior and learning.

Their model implements a predictive form of Hebbian learning through diffuse neurotransmitter systems. Its neural architecture is based on anatomical and physiological studies of bees. The proposal gives neuromodulatory signals a linked role: they can influence which actions are favored and control how synaptic connections change with experience.

The resulting model captures foraging strategies observed in bees and several other animals. This behavioral correspondence supports the proposed connection between predictive learning and action selection within the modeled architecture. The broader contribution is a unified account of how widespread chemical signals could help coordinate immediate choices with changes in future behavior. It provides a concrete computational mechanism for prediction-guided adaptation, rather than merely asserting that anticipation is useful.
neurips-1993-foraging-in-an-uncertain-en.tldr: A bee-inspired neural model uses predictive Hebbian learning and neuromodulation to reproduce animal foraging strategies under uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a network with many hidden units can still generalize well. For two-layer networks with sigmoidal hidden units, it derives a generalization-error bound involving expected network complexity, input dimension, and the number of training examples. Complexity is expressed through a random hidden-unit count bounded by the network's available units.

The distribution of that count is determined by a prior over network weights. The authors connect this prior to a Gibbs distribution associated with a regularizer. This relationship makes it possible to describe explicitly how the regularization term affects the network's balance between bias and variance.

The bound can be obtained analytically for a broad class of commonly used priors and can also help estimate expected complexity in practice. Its central implication is that the total number of available hidden units does not by itself settle the generalization question. The way regularization shapes expected complexity provides a quantitative explanation for why a large network can nevertheless predict well beyond its training data.
neurips-1993-generalization-error-and-th.tldr: A generalization bound links regularization to expected network complexity, helping explain why large networks can generalize well.

paragraphs: The paper examines learning algorithms through an optimality criterion drawn from robust control. The H-infinity criterion addresses performance when the model is uncertain and statistical information about external signals is unavailable. It offers a way to analyze robustness without depending on a fully specified statistical description of those signals.

Building on a result that the least mean squares algorithm is H-infinity optimal, the authors extend their analysis to nonlinear settings encountered in neural networks. Their central result is that backpropagation is locally optimal under the same criterion. The word locally is essential: the stated result does not assert unrestricted global optimality for nonlinear learning.

The authors interpret this connection as a theoretical explanation for the strong robustness often observed in both least mean squares and backpropagation. The contribution places familiar learning procedures within a control-theoretic account of uncertainty. It explains a particular desirable property of those algorithms through a formal criterion, while preserving the distinction between the earlier estimator result and the local nonlinear extension.
neurips-1993-hoo-optimality-criteria-for.tldr: The paper shows that backpropagation is locally H-infinity optimal, extending a robustness-based optimality result for least mean squares.

paragraphs: The paper studies face recognition under sharply changing lighting conditions. It compares images from a contrast-sensitive silicon retina with those from a conventional gain-controlled camera. The question is whether processing built into the sensor can preserve useful facial information as illumination changes.

Both inputs feed a recognition system using wavelet-based features and elastic matching. To examine the effect of the retina's analog preprocessing, the authors also digitally bandpass-filter the conventional camera images to adjust their power spectrum. This comparison considers whether sensor-level processing offers useful properties beyond that particular digital adjustment.

The authors report recognition-rate increases of up to 50 percent with the silicon retina and attribute the benefit to its adjustable sensitivity. They interpret the experiments as showing that analog on-chip preprocessing produces image data richer in features that stay associated with the object across lighting changes. The contribution therefore concerns the acquisition stage as well as recognition: changing how the image is sensed can improve the stability of the information supplied to the classifier.
neurips-1993-illumination-invariant-face.tldr: A contrast-sensitive silicon retina improves face recognition under changing illumination, with reported recognition-rate increases of up to 50 percent.

paragraphs: The paper presents electronic circuits built around the Neuron MOS transistor, also called neuMOS or vMOS. This device is designed to reproduce neuron-like behavior at the level of a single transistor. The authors use it as a building block for circuits that carry out functions associated with intelligent processing.

One example is searching a memory array for the data most similar to a query directly in hardware. Another is what the authors call Soft Hardware: circuitry whose logic function can change in real time through external control signals, without physically modifying the hardware. These examples emphasize both data-dependent selection and controllable circuit functionality.

The paper also describes a neural network with self-learning capability implemented on the chip. Together, the examples connect the proposed transistor to memory search, reconfigurable logic, and learning. The authors observe architectural similarities between the resulting circuits and biological systems. The main contribution is the implementation of these capabilities using a neuron-like device as a physical circuit primitive.
neurips-1993-implementing-intelligence-o.tldr: Neuron MOS transistors support hardware similarity search, externally reconfigurable logic, and neural circuits with on-chip learning.

paragraphs: The paper explores learning systems suited to direct digital implementation. Many neural network nodes require numerous floating-point operations, which motivates considering networks whose individual nodes instead compute simple Boolean functions. The authors investigate whether such networks can retain the ability to learn from examples and generalize.

They present two algorithms that construct Boolean networks from training examples. The reported results show strong generalization for a class of problems that can be described by compact Boolean networks. This condition matters because the favorable finding is tied to problems with an economical representation in the proposed form.

The methods are general enough to be applied even when compact Boolean structure is not known beforehand. The paper demonstrates applications to image reconstruction and handwritten character recognition. Its contribution is to connect simple digital operations with learned network behavior, showing that learning need not depend on the usual floating-point node computations. The application examples broaden the discussion beyond problems whose Boolean structure is already established.
neurips-1993-learning-complex-boolean-fu.tldr: Two algorithms learn Boolean networks from examples, generalizing well on compactly representable problems and supporting image and handwriting applications.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a computational explanation for findings that barn owl head movements are controlled by distinct circuits for horizontal and vertical motion. Those findings suggest internal coordinates aligned with meaningful directions in the external world. The question is how a learning process could produce that organization.

The proposed model uses optimal unsupervised motor learning as a framework for low-level movement learning. It supplies criteria for selecting optimal internal representations. In this account, the organization of movement commands becomes something that can be predicted from a learning objective, rather than simply taken as an observed feature of the animal.

The author reports that the theory predicts the observed results of microstimulation in barn owls. Two iterative neural network algorithms are described that find the optimal solution under the model's criteria. They provide possible mechanisms through which such internal representations could develop. The contribution links a biological pattern of movement control to a computational account of representation learning, while presenting the algorithms as candidate developmental mechanisms.
neurips-1993-optimal-unsupervised-motor-.tldr: An optimal unsupervised motor-learning model predicts barn owl movement-control findings and offers algorithms for developing the corresponding internal representation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses fault monitoring when training data cover only some of the situations a system may encounter. A classifier built from those data has an incomplete set of classes. Monitoring must therefore account for observations from unknown sources, rather than assuming every input belongs to a familiar category.

The proposed probabilistic approach combines an input-density model with a discriminative model of the known classes. These provide complementary information about the observations and their classification. Bayes' rule brings them together with prior estimates of how likely data are to come from known or unknown origins, producing classification equations that explicitly allow novelty.

The authors apply this approach with hidden Markov models to online monitoring of large ground antennas used for spacecraft tracking. The application particularly concerns transient behavior of unknown origin. Its significance is that recognizing known faults and detecting unfamiliar behavior become parts of the same probabilistic treatment. The stated need for prior known-versus-unknown likelihood estimates is part of that formulation.
neurips-1993-probabilistic-anomaly-detec.tldr: The paper combines density and class models to detect unfamiliar behavior during probabilistic fault monitoring of dynamic systems.

paragraphs: The paper tackles cursive handwriting by using recognition to help decide where letters begin and end. Joined writing admits multiple possible segmentations, so the system considers letter recognition and word segmentation together. It operates on online handwriting, where the input is a stream of pen coordinates.

The coordinate stream is converted into a sequence of uniform stroke descriptions. Six feed-forward neural networks process these descriptions, with different networks intended to recognize letters of different sizes. A best-first search then explores possible segmentations to recognize the word. This makes the choice of segmentation depend on the recognition process rather than fixing all boundaries in advance.

The study uses a database of 10,000 English words. Reported error rates range from 1.7% to 15.5% for writer-dependent recognition and from 5.2% to 31.1% for writer-independent recognition. These findings demonstrate the method in both settings while showing different reported ranges. The central contribution is the combination of stroke encoding, multiple letter recognizers, and search over alternative word segmentations.
neurips-1993-recognition-based-segmentat.tldr: Six neural letter recognizers and best-first search jointly segment and recognize online cursive words.

paragraphs: The paper proposes nonlinear learning models that can be solved mathematically. Its purpose is to make aspects of neural network learning accessible to direct analysis, rather than relying only on observed training behavior. The authors study learning using the theory of ordinary differential equations.

Within these solvable models, they construct a learning algorithm that finds an optimal parameter without a recursive procedure. This provides a setting in which the relationship between the model, its parameters, and the learning solution can be examined explicitly. The claim concerns the proposed solvable models; it is not presented as a universal solution for arbitrary neural networks.

The models are also used to investigate why experimental results from error backpropagation can appear to contradict statistical learning theory. Their value is therefore explanatory as well as algorithmic. A mathematically tractable learning system offers a way to study the source of that disagreement and connect training behavior with theoretical expectations. The abstract states this analytical purpose without specifying the resulting explanation.
neurips-1993-solvable-models-of-artifici.tldr: Solvable nonlinear learning models enable nonrecursive parameter optimization and analysis of apparent disagreements between backpropagation experiments and learning theory.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how structured neural activity can emerge from independently supplied noise. Its model is a two-dimensional sheet of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, connected through nearby excitation and surrounding inhibition. Although the external drive is homogeneous, the network spontaneously develops localized regions of stronger activity.

These hotspots form clusters that merge, break apart, change size, and move in constrained random walks. Their interactions produce correlations across long time intervals. Correlations between units have two components: a narrow peak near simultaneous activity and a much broader underlying rise. The model thus produces structure on more than one temporal scale.

The frequency patterns differ between individual neurons and population activity. Single units show 1/f behavior at low frequencies and a flat spectrum at higher frequencies. Activity averaged over many cells instead lacks that 1/f decay and shows a pronounced peak near 40 Hz. This distinction matters because population averaging changes which collective dynamics are visible, even though both measurements come from the same modeled network.
neurips-1993-synchronization-oscillation.tldr: A noisy spiking network develops moving activity clusters, with low-frequency 1/f behavior in single neurons and a roughly 40 Hz peak in population activity.
